content.stem: Which of the following pillars of Total Productive Maintenance (TPM) allows machine operators to gain more knowledge about and take greater ownership of their equipment?
content.why: Pillar 1 — autonomous maintenance allows machine operators to gain more knowledge about and take greater ownership of their equipment. Pillar 3 focuses on the quality aspect of maintenance and preventing defects from moving down the value chain. A. Pillar 1 - autonomous maintenance Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Control Phase, Question 10 (PDF p. 118).

options: Employees receive long, written descriptions of processes and procedures.
Work stays in process for a longer amount of time.
Errors are completely removed from the process.
content.stem: Which of the following is a benefit of implementing a visual factory?
content.why: A visual factory makes hazards, safe areas, status, and instructions immediately visible, which supports a safer workplace. C. A safer workplace is created. Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Control Phase, Question 11 (PDF p. 118).

options: The change is both statistically and practically significant.
The change is practically significant but not statistically significant.
The change is statistically significant but may not be practically significant.
The p-value proves that the process change caused the reduction.
content.stem: A process change reduces average cycle time from 60.0 to 59.8 minutes. With a very large sample, the test returns p = 0.001, but customers will not notice a 0.2-minute reduction. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
content.why: The small p-value provides evidence of a real difference, but practical significance depends on whether the effect is large enough to matter operationally or to customers. A p-value does not establish causation. C. The change is statistically significant but may not be practically significant. Source: ASQ CSSGB Body of Knowledge (2022), IV.B.1 - statistical and practical significance.

options: Use a smaller practical effect size while keeping the sample unchanged.
Add measurement error to make the data more variable.
content.stem: A hypothesis test has insufficient power to detect a practically important difference. If all other planning assumptions remain unchanged, which action most directly increases the test's power?
content.why: Increasing sample size reduces standard error and raises the probability of detecting the specified effect when it truly exists. Smaller samples and greater measurement variation reduce power. B. Increase the sample size. Source: ASQ CSSGB Body of Knowledge (2022), IV.B.1 - sample size and power.

content.stem: A team repeatedly asks why a packaging seal failed. Each answer becomes the basis for the next question until the team reaches an inadequate preventive-maintenance standard. Which root-cause tool is the team using?
content.why: The 5 Whys technique follows a causal chain by repeatedly asking why the preceding condition occurred. It aims to move beyond the visible symptom toward an actionable root cause. A. 5 Whys Source: ASQ CSSGB Body of Knowledge (2022), IV.C.2 - root cause analysis.

options: The factors do not affect the response.
The effect of one factor depends on the level of the other factor.
Only a main effect is present.
content.stem: On a two-factor interaction plot, the response lines for Factors A and B are clearly nonparallel and cross. What does this pattern indicate?
content.why: Nonparallel lines indicate interaction: the effect of one factor changes across levels of the other factor. Crossing lines are a strong visual signal of such dependence. B. The effect of one factor depends on the level of the other factor. Source: ASQ CSSGB Body of Knowledge (2022), V.A.2 - interaction plots.

content.stem: Before deploying a redesigned scheduling process across 20 plants, the team runs it for four weeks at one representative plant using real employees and real transactions. What implementation method is this?
content.why: A pilot test applies the proposed solution on a limited real-world scale before broader deployment. A simulation models behavior without implementing the complete process in normal operations. B. Pilot test Source: ASQ CSSGB Body of Knowledge (2022), V.B - implementation planning.

options: It maximizes variation within each subgroup.
It makes parts within a subgroup likely to be produced under similar conditions while allowing hour-to-hour shifts to appear between subgroups.
It guarantees that every manufactured part is inspected.
It eliminates the need to investigate special causes.
content.stem: A machining process is sampled by taking five consecutive parts every hour. Why is this a rational subgrouping strategy?
content.why: Rational subgroups are formed so within-subgroup observations reflect short-term common-cause variation, while meaningful changes over time appear between subgroups. B. It makes parts within a subgroup likely to be produced under similar conditions while allowing hour-to-hour shifts to appear between subgroups. Source: ASQ CSSGB Body of Knowledge (2022), VI.A.2 - rational subgrouping.

options: Leave both versions at the workstation so operators can choose.
Remove obsolete controlled copies, identify the current revision, and retain superseded versions only according to the retention procedure.
Rely on verbal notice without changing the revision identifier.
Delete every historical version immediately, regardless of retention requirements.
content.stem: A revised work instruction is approved and released. Which action best supports document control and prevents operators from using the obsolete version?
content.why: Effective document control makes the approved revision identifiable and available at the point of use while preventing unintended use of obsolete copies. Retention requirements still govern archived versions. B. Remove obsolete controlled copies, identify the current revision, and retain superseded versions only according to the retention procedure. Source: ASQ CSSGB Body of Knowledge (2022), VI.B.2 - document control.

content.stem: A customer audits one of its key suppliers to verify conformance with contractual quality requirements. What type of audit is this?
content.why: A second-party audit is performed by an interested external party, commonly a customer auditing a supplier. First-party audits are internal; independent certification bodies conduct third-party audits. B. Second-party audit Source: ASQ CSSGB Body of Knowledge (2022), VI.B.4 - audits.

options: Define, Measure, Analyze, Design, and Verify (DMADV).
content.sourceSection: Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: Which methodology is most commonly used for Design for Six Sigma (DFSS)?
content.why: Define, Measure, Analyze, Design, and Verify (DMADV) is the most popular Design for Six Sigma methodology. Identify, Design, Optimize, and Verify (IDOV) focuses heavily on the voice of the customer and how to accurately, effectively, and efficiently translate that into a final product. A. Define, Measure, Analyze, Design, and Verify (DMADV). Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 10 (PDF p. 28).

options: Return to Plan without documenting the result.
Act by standardizing the successful change and determining the next improvement cycle.
Do by repeating the trial without reviewing it.
Check by developing the original problem statement.
content.stem: During PDCA, a trial solution has been implemented and its results have been compared with the target. The target was achieved. What should the team do next?
content.why: After Check confirms that the trial achieved its objective, Act institutionalizes the successful method through standards, training, and controls, then feeds learning into the next cycle. B. Act by standardizing the successful change and determining the next improvement cycle. Source: ASQ CSSGB Body of Knowledge (2022), VI.B.5 - PDCA.

content.sourceSection: Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: During a Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), severity is rated 8, occurrence is rated 10, and detection is rated 6. What is the risk priority number (RPN)?
content.why: RPN = Severity × Occurrence × Detection = 8 × 10 × 6 = 480. A. 480 Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 11 (PDF p. 28).

content.sourceSection: Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: During a Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), severity is rated 5, occurrence is rated 7, and detection is rated 9. What is the criticality?
content.why: 35 is the criticality. The criticality is calculated by multiplying together the severity and the occurrence ratings (5 x 7). C. 35 Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 12 (PDF p. 28).

options: Metrics are financial and non-financial in nature.
Metrics span the financial, customer, internal-process, and learning-and-growth perspectives.
Measurements can include both leading and lagging indicators.
Metrics are only reflective of efforts around customer loyalty initiatives.
content.sourceSection: Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of the design of a balanced scorecard?
content.why: A balanced scorecard spans financial, customer, internal-process, and learning-and-growth perspectives; it is not limited to customer loyalty. D. Metrics are only reflective of efforts around customer loyalty initiatives. Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 13 (PDF p. 28).

content.stem: What is a series of steps that transforms inputs into outputs?
content.why: A process is a linked series of steps that converts inputs into outputs. A. Process Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 1 (PDF p. 44).

content.stem: What type of benchmarking takes place when a group of universities forms an association to allow its members to provide information to the association?
content.why: Collaborative benchmarking takes place as part of a group and is exhibited in this question’s example. Internal benchmarking takes place when comparable industries aren’t easily available, or when an organization wishes to share its established and proven best practices. C. Collaborative Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 2 (PDF p. 44).

options: Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, and Customers (SIPOC) diagram
Program evaluation and review technique (PERT) chart
content.stem: Which tool is used by a Six Sigma project team to further define a project that hasn’t been thoroughly scoped?
content.why: A SIPOC diagram is a tool that’s used by a Six Sigma project team to further define a project that hasn’t been thoroughly scoped. QFD is the systematic approach used to translate customer requirements into actual design characteristics during each stage of product or service development. B. Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, and Customers (SIPOC) diagram Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 3 (PDF p. 44).

content.stem: Which is the best data collection technique to use when there’s a desire to reach a large number of people while trying to minimize cost?
content.why: A survey can reach many people at relatively low cost. Focus groups and individual interviews involve fewer participants and generally require more coordination per participant. D. Survey Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 4 (PDF p. 44).

content.stem: What’s sometimes referred to as the voice of the customer being translated into the voice of the engineer?
content.why: Quality Function Deployment (QFD) is sometimes referred to as the voice of the customer being translated into the voice of the engineer. The Voice of the Customer (VOC) is what’s being translated for the project. C. Quality Function Deployment (QFD) Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 5 (PDF p. 44).

content.stem: What document defines the boundaries of the Six Sigma project, sets limits on what is and isn’t included, and helps keep the project team focused, motivated, and aligned?
content.why: Project scope is the document that defines the boundaries of the Six Sigma project and sets limits on what is and isn’t included in the project, which helps to keep the project team focused, motivated, and aligned. Project metrics are used to compare the baseline to the improvement level at the close of the project. A. Project scope Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 6 (PDF p. 44).

content.sourceSection: Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: Which Six Sigma quality leader is known for the 80/20 rule, where 20 percent of the defects ultimately lead to 80 percent of the problems?
content.why: Juran is associated with the Pareto principle: a vital few causes account for a large share of the effects. C. Dr. Joseph M. Juran Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 1 (PDF p. 27).

content.stem: Which of the following elements is NOT typically included in the project charter?
content.why: A process map typically isn’t included in the project charter. Process maps are usually constructed later, as a tool within the project. B. Process map Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 7 (PDF p. 44).

content.stem: What are metrics that quantify positive side effects resulting from a process improvement after accomplishing a primary metric known as?
content.why: Secondary metrics quantify positive side effects that result from a process improvement after accomplishing a primary metric. Consequential metrics are used to measure negative side effects that can unintentionally result from Six Sigma projects, such as process defects or problems. B. Secondary metrics Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 8 (PDF p. 45).

content.stem: Which chart uses a network diagram of numbered nodes representing project milestones which are linked together by labeled vectors representing project tasks?
content.why: A PERT chart represents milestones as nodes and project tasks as the links between them. B. PERT chart Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 9 (PDF p. 45).

content.stem: A company lists a threat of the rent for one of its properties increasing by $12,000 a month in the coming year, with a 50 percent chance of the threat occurring. What’s the associated risk value?
content.why: Annual exposure is $12,000 × 12 = $144,000; multiplying by 50% probability gives a $72,000 risk value. D. $72,000 Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 10 (PDF p. 45).

options: Hold a milestone celebration for the project team
content.stem: Which of the following is the final step in the project closure process?
content.why: The source treats the post-implementation review as the final closure step after notification, documentation, and celebration activities. B. Conduct a post implementation review (PIR) Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 11 (PDF p. 45).

content.stem: Which tool is used to successively break down and analyze a process into increasingly finer levels of detail and is good for a project team to use when working to get to the root cause of a problem?
content.why: A tree diagram decomposes a problem into progressively finer levels, helping a team work toward root causes. C. Tree diagram Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 12 (PDF p. 45).

content.stem: Which tool is used to demonstrate cause-and-effect relationships and to assist a project team with analyzing the links involved in a complex situation?
content.why: An interrelationship digraph makes cause-and-effect links in a complex situation visible. A. Interrelationship digraph Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 13 (PDF p. 45).

content.stem: Which tool is used to identify elements that can go wrong in a proposed plan that’s large, must be completed on schedule, and has a high price of failure?
content.why: A process decision program chart anticipates what could go wrong in a high-risk plan and identifies countermeasures. D. Process decision program chart Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 14 (PDF p. 45).

content.stem: Which tool is used to show the relationships of the major project steps in sequence using nodes and arrows?
content.why: An activity network diagram shows the relationships of the major steps in the project in sequence using nodes and arrows. A process decision program chart is used to identify elements that can go wrong in a proposed plan that’s large, must be completed on schedule, and has a high price of failure. C. Activity network diagram Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 15 (PDF p. 46).

content.stem: If 30 defects are found in 200 units of product, what’s the DPU (defects per unit)?
content.why: DPU = total defects ÷ total units = 30 ÷ 200 = 0.15. C. 0.15 DPU Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 16 (PDF p. 46).

content.sourceSection: Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: Which Six Sigma quality leader is known for his 14 Points for Management that serves as a guide about what to change?
content.why: Deming formulated the 14 Points for Management as guidance for organizational transformation. D. Dr. W. Edwards Deming Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 2 (PDF p. 27).

content.stem: A college admission form has 25 fields of information. If 10 forms are sampled and 15 defects are found, what is the DPMO (defects per million opportunities)?
content.why: DPMO = 15 ÷ (10 × 25) × 1,000,000 = 60,000. A. 60,000 DPMO Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 17 (PDF p. 46).

content.stem: If the first step in a process has a daily yield of 80%, the second step has a daily yield of 90%, and the third step has a daily yield of 75%, what’s the rolled throughput yield (RTY)?
content.why: RTY is the product of the step yields: 0.80 × 0.90 × 0.75 = 0.54, or 54%. B. 54% Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 18 (PDF p. 46).

content.stem: What type of communication tends to be one-directional in nature and doesn’t require a response from the recipient?
content.why: Top-down communication commonly flows in one direction from leadership and may not require a response. C. Top-down communication Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 19 (PDF p. 46).

content.stem: Two employees on the same team are working together to solve a problem for a customer. They work in the same office space and talk in-depth about the different solutions they could offer the customer. What type of communication is this?
content.why: Communication between colleagues at the same organizational level is lateral communication. D. Lateral communication Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 20 (PDF p. 46).

content.stem: During which stage of team development do team members find it relatively easy to be part of the team and can be seen taking on various roles and responsibilities as needed?
content.why: In the performing stage, members work effectively and take on roles as the team requires. A. Performing Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 21 (PDF p. 46).

content.stem: During which stage of team development might a team member be impolite when expressing frustrations about expectations toward another team member?
content.why: During the storming stage of team development, a team member may be impolite when expressing frustrations about expectations toward another team member. During the performing stage of team development, team members find it relatively easy to be part of the team and can be seen taking on various roles and responsibilities as needed. B. Storming Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 22 (PDF p. 47).

content.stem: Which role assists the team when disputes arise in a Six Sigma project, encourages members to voice their opinions, and helps the parties involved move beyond an impasse by collaborating effectively?
content.why: A facilitator assists the team when disputes arise, encourages members to voice their opinions, and helps the parties move beyond an impasse through effective collaboration. C. Facilitator Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Define Phase, Question 23 (PDF p. 47).

content.stem: Which study directly evaluates both equipment repeatability and appraiser reproducibility in a measurement system?
content.why: A gage repeatability and reproducibility (Gage R&R) study separates measurement-system variation into equipment variation (repeatability) and appraiser variation (reproducibility). B. Gage R&R worksheets Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 1 (PDF p. 70), clarified for a single defensible answer.

content.stem: Financial capital, personnel required, time spent, materials used, and labor expended are examples of which of the following process aspects?
content.why: Project costs aren’t always limited to actual dollars spent. Costs also involve human expenditure, material expenditure, and time. A. Project costs Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 2 (PDF p. 70).

content.stem: Which measure for the center of a small sample set would be most affected by outliers?
content.why: Mean. An outlier is a data value that’s either far above or below the majority of values in a sample set. A. Mean Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 3 (PDF p. 70).

content.sourceSection: Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: What diagram is used to brainstorm all possible causes of a problem in order to sort ideas into categories that ultimately lead to a solution?
content.why: The fishbone diagram is used to brainstorm all possible causes of a problem so that ideas can be sorted into categories that ultimately lead to a solution. The Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) cycle is an ongoing evaluation of procedures and managerial policies leading to continuous improvement, and it is made up of four stages. B. Fishbone diagram Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 3 (PDF p. 27).

content.stem: Estimation and hypothesis testing are the two main types of which of the following?
content.why: Inferential statistics. Estimation and hypothesis testing are the two main types of inferential statistics, which are used to analyze the strength of the relationship between independent and dependent variables. C. Inferential statistics Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 4 (PDF p. 70).

content.stem: A box-and-whisker plot of yearly salaries for car salespersons has Q1 = $45,000, Q2 = $51,000, and Q3 = $59,000. Which of the following salaries would be considered outliers? I. $21,000 II. $28,000 III. $65,000 IV. $85,000
content.why: IQR = $59,000 − $45,000 = $14,000. The fences are $24,000 and $80,000, so $21,000 and $85,000 are outliers. C. I and IV Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 5 (PDF p. 70).

options: The sampling distribution of the mean always has the same shape as the population.
A sample size of 20 always produces exactly the same sampling distribution as a sample size of 30.
As sample size increases, the sampling distribution of a sum or mean tends toward a normal distribution under the theorem's usual conditions, even when the population is non-normal.
content.stem: Which statement best describes the Central Limit Theorem?
content.why: The Central Limit Theorem states that, under its usual independence and finite-variance conditions, the sampling distribution of a sum or mean approaches normality as sample size increases. A sample size of 30 is only a common rule of thumb; the required size depends on the population's shape. C. As sample size increases, the sampling distribution of a sum or mean tends toward a normal distribution under the theorem's usual conditions, even when the population is non-normal. Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 6 (PDF p. 70), clarified for statistical accuracy.

options: The system has a poor repeatability rating.
content.stem: A measurement system used to quantify mass produces an average measurement of 48 g for a product with a true mass of 51 g. The same system produces an average of 107 g for a part with a true mass of 105 g. What can be said about the measurement system?
content.why: The system lacks linearity. Linearity refers to the consistency of the bias (the difference between the average measured values and the true values) throughout the range of the system. C. The system lacks linearity. Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 7 (PDF p. 71).

options: Both typical and atypical causes can affect a process and lead to variations within the process that may prevent its goals from being achieved.
Both typical and atypical causes are identified and removed prior to determining and computing process capability.
Process capability is defined as how effective a process is at meeting the desired goals and objectives.
content.stem: Which of the following statements regarding process capability is false?
content.why: Statement B is false. Special (atypical) causes should be identified and removed before capability is interpreted, but common-cause variation is inherent in a stable process and is not simply removed before the calculation. B. Both typical and atypical causes are identified and removed prior to determining and computing process capability. Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 8 (PDF p. 71), corrected for statistical accuracy.

content.stem: Which of the following measures the difference between actual and estimated amounts, is most commonly used in inferential statistics, and is the sum of squared z-scores, or normal deviates?
content.why: Chi-square distributions. Chi-square distributions measure the difference between actual and estimated amounts, and are commonly used in inferential statistics. C. Chi-square distributions Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 9 (PDF p. 71).

options: There is a weak negative correlation.
There is a weak positive correlation.
There is a strong positive correlation.
content.stem: A scatter diagram is constructed to represent the mileage of a car and its cumulative maintenance cost. Without seeing the diagram, you’re told that its correlation coefficient, r, has been calculated to be 0.96. What can you tell about the two variables (mileage and cumulative maintenance costs)?
content.why: There is a strong positive correlation. The correlation coefficient, r, for a scatter diagram has a value between -1 and 1, where r is positive for a positive correlation and negative for a negative correlation. D. There is a strong positive correlation. Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 10 (PDF p. 71).

content.stem: A company wants to analyze employee satisfaction by department. Its population contains 160,352 employees across 12 departments, but the population data are not currently separated by department. Which sampling method is most appropriate?
content.why: Stratified. Stratified sampling is utilized when there is no conformity within a population, and the population must first be subdivided before samples can be taken. B. Stratified Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 11 (PDF p. 71).

content.stem: A sample modeled by a normal distribution for football players' weekly training time has a mean of 21 hours and a standard deviation of 2.5 hours. What is the probability that a randomly chosen player practices at least 16 hours per week?
content.why: 16 hours is two standard deviations below the mean: z = (16 − 21) ÷ 2.5 = −2. About 97.5% of observations lie at or above z = −2. A. 97.5% Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 12 (PDF p. 72).

content.stem: Which of the following analyzes and measures the following components: process steps, potential failure mode, potential failure causes and effects, failure severity, occurrence, and risk priority?
content.why: FMEA matrix. A FMEA matrix, also known as failure mode and effects analysis, is a tool that analyzes factors contributing to a failing process or product, as well as the effects of those failures. C. FMEA matrix Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 13 (PDF p. 72).

content.sourceSection: Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: Which category is NOT one of the perspectives that metrics span across on a balanced scorecard?
content.why: Environmental is NOT one of the four perspectives that metrics span across on a balanced scorecard. The four perspectives are: financial, customer, internal business processes, and employee learning and growth. A. Environmental Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 4 (PDF p. 27).

options: The system is accurate and precise.
The system is accurate but not precise.
The system is precise but not accurate.
The system is neither accurate nor precise.
content.stem: After analyzing a measurement system, it’s determined that the measurements are close to each other but not close to the true value of the sample. Which of the following would describe the system?
content.why: The system is precise but not accurate. The accuracy of a system refers to how close the measurements it produces are to their accepted reference values, or true values. C. The system is precise but not accurate. Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 14 (PDF p. 72).

options: There is not an equal probability of all units being selected when utilizing random sampling methods.
This method requires extensive information about the population being sampled.
This method can be used when little information is provided about the population being sampled.
content.stem: Which of the following statements is true about random sampling?
content.why: Random sampling entails randomly drawing an item so that every item drawn has an equal chance of being included in the sample. In other words, there is an equal probability with random sampling. C. This method can be used when little information is provided about the population being sampled. Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 15 (PDF p. 72).

content.stem: A problem with a measurement device would show up in an assessment for which of the following?
content.why: Repeatability is equipment variation observed when the same appraiser measures the same parts repeatedly with the same device. Reproducibility is variation between appraisers. A. Repeatability Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 16 (PDF p. 72).

options: Employees working on an assembly line
Number of defective units per batch
Number of parts to a unit
content.stem: Which of the following represents an example of discrete data?
content.why: Each example is a count and therefore takes distinct whole-number values. Counts are discrete data. D. All of the above Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 17 (PDF p. 72).

options: Cp and Cpk values equal to 1 represent a process that is barely capable and barely meeting specifications.
When a process is centered, Cp and Cpk are equal.
Cp and Cpk values less than 1 represent a process that is capable and meeting specifications.
content.stem: Which of the following statements regarding process capability ratio (Cp) and centered process capability ratio (Cpk) is factual?
content.why: When a process is centered, its potential capability Cp equals its centered capability Cpk. B. When a process is centered, Cp and Cpk are equal. Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 18 (PDF p. 72).

options: The results of credit card applications (approved or rejected), with a sample of 60 from 758 applicants.
The lengths of pieces of lumber with a sample set of 102 from 508 total pieces.
The time required for each of 47 students to complete a certification exam.
The weight of babies born at a hospital in 2015, with a sample of 92 from 215 babies.
content.stem: Which of the following scenarios is appropriately modeled using a binomial distribution?
content.why: A binomial model applies to a fixed number of trials with two outcomes per trial and a constant probability of success. Each sampled credit application is classified as approved or rejected; the remaining choices are continuous measurements. A. The results of credit card applications (approved or rejected), with a sample of 60 from 758 applicants. Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 19 (PDF p. 73), clarified for a single defensible answer.

content.stem: Which of the following is an illustrative tool to represent a detailed view of inputs, outputs, actions, decision points, sequencing, and process steps?
content.why: Process mapping. A process map includes each step involved in a process and comprises of inputs, process steps, and outputs. D. Process mapping Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 20 (PDF p. 73).

content.stem: What is the probability that a random data point chosen from a standard normal distribution falls between z = -0.03 and z = 0.25? (Use cumulative areas 0.4880 and 0.5987, respectively.)
content.why: Using the corrected cumulative areas, P(−0.03 < Z < 0.25) = 0.5987 − 0.4880 = 0.1107, or approximately 11%. The printed guide's 0.3483 value and 25% key are inconsistent with the standard normal distribution. B. Approximately 11% Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 21 (PDF p. 73).

content.stem: Which of the following sampling methods would be utilized when a high unit cost is present, and the approach is to test individual units one by one until the desired testing results are achieved?
content.why: Sequential. Sequential sampling is often used in quality control testing where a higher cost is associated with testing the units in the sample. A. Sequential Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 22 (PDF p. 73).

content.stem: A six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability that the roll is 1 or 2?
content.why: Two of the six equally likely outcomes are favorable, so P(1 or 2) = 2/6 = 1/3. C. 1/3 Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 23 (PDF p. 73).

content.sourceSection: Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: What’s the goal of the Theory of Constraints?
content.why: The goal of the Theory of Constraints is to increase profits by pinpointing constraints that exist in any component of the process. This theory is constructed on the premise that, in any context, at least one constraint exists that holds back profits from being as high as possible. D. Increase profits Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 5 (PDF p. 27).

options: The process is well centered because Pp and Ppk are equal.
The process has adequate potential spread but is poorly centered relative to the specifications.
The process is unstable because Ppk is lower than Pp.
The process mean is exactly on the target.
content.stem: A stable, approximately normal process has Pp = 1.50 and Ppk = 0.90. Which conclusion is best supported?
content.why: Pp describes potential performance based on overall spread, while Ppk also reflects centering. A much smaller Ppk indicates that the process mean is too close to one specification limit; it does not by itself prove instability. B. The process has adequate potential spread but is poorly centered relative to the specifications. Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Measure Phase, Question 24 (PDF p. 73), clarified for a single defensible answer.

content.stem: Minitab and Stata are all examples of which of the following?
content.why: Minitab and Stata are statistical software packages used to analyze data and produce statistical output. They are not statistical theorems or spreadsheet-specific applications. A. Statistical software Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Analyze Phase, Question 1 (PDF p. 89).

content.stem: Which of the following describes a tool utilized for testing the variables for relationships in either direction, and divides the alpha error into two equal parts within the distribution when testing for statistical significance?
content.why: Two-tail test. A two-tail test, also referred to as a non-directional hypothesis, tests the variables for relationships in either direction. C. Two-tail test Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Analyze Phase, Question 2 (PDF p. 89).

content.stem: A line that travels from the bottom-left of a graph to the upper-right of the graph indicates what kind of relationship between a predictor and a dependent variable?
content.why: This vector indicates linear relationships of positive notation. A negative relationship would show points traveling from the top-left of the graph to the bottom-right. A. Positive Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Analyze Phase, Question 3 (PDF p. 89).

options: The predictor variable directly causes the presence of the outcome being studied
A non-linear relationship, usually in a parabolic shape
content.stem: What does a correlation coefficient of 1 indicate between a predictor variable and a dependent variable?
content.why: Correlation coefficients can range from -1, the strongest possible negative relationship, to 1, the strongest possible positive relationship. A correlation coefficient of 0 indicates no relationship. B. The strongest possible positive relationship Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Analyze Phase, Question 4 (PDF p. 89).

content.stem: Which of the following indicate the notation used for the correlation coefficient in a simple regression analysis and a multiple regression analysis, respectively?
content.why: A lowercase r indicates that this correlation coefficient describes the relationship between one predictor variable and one dependent variable. An uppercase R indicates that this correlation coefficient describes the relationship between multiple predictor variables and a dependent variable. C. r, R Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Analyze Phase, Question 5 (PDF p. 89).

content.stem: Which of the following terms describes when two or more predictor variables have a high correlation, making it difficult to determine relationships between one or more predictor variables and the dependent variable(s)?
content.why: Multicollinearity describes when two or more predictor variables may have a significant relationship with the outcome being studied, and it’s difficult to tell which predictor variable is influencing the outcome. Multicollinearity typically takes place within multiple regression analyses, but not all multiple regression analyses experience this phenomenon. D. Multicollinearity Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Analyze Phase, Question 6 (PDF p. 89).

options: There’s a negative/inverse relationship between the variables.
Some points in the data set are identified as outliers.
There’s a positive/direct relationship between the variables.
A relationship exists between the variables, but a linear regression technique cannot explain it.
content.stem: When a data set plots as a non-linear shape (such as a cluster or curve), what does this indicate about the relationship between the predictor and dependent variables?
content.why: When a data set plots as a non-linear shape, this means that a relationship exists between the predictor and dependent variables. However, a linear regression technique doesn’t help to explain the relationship. D. A relationship exists between the variables, but a linear regression technique cannot explain it. Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Analyze Phase, Question 7 (PDF p. 90).

content.stem: Which of the following is an example of cyclical process variation?
content.why: Cyclical variation is also referred to as part-to-part or lot-to-lot variation, and tracks variations from unit to unit. Temporal variation is also referred to as shift-to-shift variation, and tracks time-related variations. B. Part-to-part variation Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Analyze Phase, Question 8 (PDF p. 90).

content.stem: Which of the following hypothesis tests requires equal sample sizes?
content.why: Paired t-test. The paired t-test matches each data point in one sample with a data point in another sample to determine the difference. C. Paired T-test Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Analyze Phase, Question 9 (PDF p. 90).

content.sourceSection: Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: Which is NOT one of the five principles of lean thinking?
content.why: The five Lean thinking principles are value, value stream, flow, pull, and perfection. Employee satisfaction can be an important organizational outcome, but it is not one of these five named principles. C. Employee satisfaction Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 6 (PDF p. 27), clarified for a single defensible answer.

options: The time scale is placed along the vertical axis, and the values are placed along the horizontal axis; the length of each vertical line represents variations within the samples.
The time scale is placed along the horizontal axis, and the values are placed along the vertical axis; the position of vertical lines represents variations within the samples.
The time scale is placed along the vertical axis, and the values are placed along the horizontal axis; the position of vertical lines represents variations from sample to sample.
content.stem: Which of the following accurately describes a multi-variate line chart used for detecting and tracking process variations?
content.why: In a multi-vari chart, the horizontal axis represents time, vertical position shows sample-to-sample variation, and the length of each vertical line shows within-sample variation. None of A–C states all three correctly. D. None of the above. Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Analyze Phase, Question 10 (PDF p. 90).

content.stem: A toothpaste company proclaims that 90% of U.S. dentists recommend its brand. You poll a random sample of 100 dentists and 83 recommend the brand. Which test can determine whether the company's statement is false?
content.why: One-sample proportion test. A one-sample proportion test can determine if the proportion of a sample set is significantly different from a given proportion of its population. A. One-sample proportion test Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Analyze Phase, Question 11 (PDF p. 90).

content.stem: Which of the following indicates a false positive, occurring when the null hypothesis is incorrectly rejected?
content.why: A false positive is a Type I (alpha) error: rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true. C. Type I error Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Analyze Phase, Question 12 (PDF p. 90).

content.stem: In an acceptance decision, the null hypothesis is that the product is non-defective. If the product is judged non-defective when it is actually defective, which error has occurred?
content.why: The decision fails to reject a false null hypothesis, so it is a Type II (beta or false-negative) error. A. Type II error Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Analyze Phase, Question 13 (PDF p. 91), clarified by stating the null hypothesis.

options: A or B may apply; more information is required
content.stem: If the significance level is 0.05 and the p-value is 0.02, then the test is considered to be which of the following?
content.why: Statistically significant. Statistical significance translates to rejecting the null hypothesis; in other words, it correlates to the probability of a relationship existing between the variables and samples rather than being due to sampling error or chance. B. Statistically significant Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Analyze Phase, Question 14 (PDF p. 91).

options: Comparing the marital status of adults of different ethnic groups.
Comparing the average length of marriage of different ethnic groups.
Comparing the number of injuries per month at different manufacturing plants.
Comparing the test scores for employees before and after training.
content.stem: Which of the following scenarios can be tested using the chi-square test for a contingency table?
content.why: Compare the marital status of adults of different ethnic groups. The chi-square test fora contingency table can determine whether there is a difference between the distributions of two categorical variables. A. Comparing the marital status of adults of different ethnic groups. Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Analyze Phase, Question 15 (PDF p. 91).

content.stem: The concept of lean manufacturing was originally developed and introduced by which of the following organizations?
content.why: Toyota Motor Corporation developed Lean from just-in-time manufacturing principles to conserve valuable resources through small operational changes. Lean systems describe systems that are able to maximize production while minimizing the amount of non-financial, valuable resources used. A. Toyota Motor Corporation Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Improve Phase, Question 1 (PDF p. 102).

content.stem: Marcy is a manufacturing engineer for a global company. She has to make multiple copies of protocols regularly for her lab, so she walks to the copier almost hourly. The copier is located on the other side of her large building. This process is wasteful in terms of which aspect of lean methodology?
content.why: Motion includes waste related to employee effort and movement. Marcy could be more efficient if the copy machine was located near her workspace, or if she made all of her copies at one time during the day. C. Motion Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Improve Phase, Question 2 (PDF p. 102).

content.stem: In English, the 5S system stands for which of the following terms?
content.why: Sort, Set, Shine, Standardize, and Sustain define a system intended to help organizations standardize, organize, and optimize its practices and standard of cleanliness. These aspects also contribute to overall workplace and occupational safety for employees. B. Sort, Set, Shine, Standardize, Sustain Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Improve Phase, Question 3 (PDF p. 102).

content.stem: Joe holds a continuous improvement event for his manufacturing team to streamline an existing process. For some reason, his team produces too many units. He brings in a whiteboard and different colored cards to signify each component of the process as they occur. He divides the board into rows to show what happens before production, during production, and after production. Joe is using which of the following tools to help his team?
content.why: A Kanban system almost always uses a board, or cards on a board, as a visual aid to illustrate process flow. This system focuses on scheduling tasks in an operational process to control inventory and streamline the manufacturing and supply chain. A. Kanban Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Improve Phase, Question 4 (PDF p. 102).

content.sourceSection: Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: Which of the following is a visual means to identify and analyze a specific business process within a company?
content.why: Value stream mapping is a visual means to identify and analyze a specific business process within a company. An Ishikawa/fishbone diagram is used to brainstorm all possible causes of a problem to sort ideas into categories that ultimately lead to a solution. A. Value stream mapping Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 7 (PDF p. 27).

content.stem: A team studies whether hours of preparation affect exam scores. Which variable is the independent variable?
content.why: The independent variable is the input or predictor deliberately varied or observed to evaluate its relationship with the response. Exam score and the other outcome measures are dependent variables. B. Hours of preparation Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Improve Phase, Question 5 (PDF p. 102), clarified for a single defensible answer.

content.stem: A two-level full-factorial DOE with four factors is written as 2⁴. How many factor-level combinations are required?
content.why: A 2^4 full-factorial design has 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 factor-level combinations. C. 16 Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Improve Phase, Question 6 (PDF p. 102).

content.stem: When changes are made to a factor’s settings that result in a change to the response, it is known as which of the following?
content.why: When changes are made to a factor’s setting that result in a change to the response, it is known as effect. Levels are the settings for each factor in an experiment, such as temperature. A. Effect Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Improve Phase, Question 7 (PDF p. 103).

content.stem: Which of the following terms means the entire set of combinations is repeated after all of the runs are finished?
content.why: Replication occurs when the entire set of treatment combinations is repeated after the original runs are finished. Conducting experimental runs in a random order is randomization. D. Replication Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Improve Phase, Question 8 (PDF p. 103).

content.stem: In DOE, the effect that an independent variable has on a dependent variable averaging across the levels of any other independent variables is known as which of the following?
content.why: A main effect is one factor's average effect on the response across the levels of the other factors. B. Main effect Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Improve Phase, Question 9 (PDF p. 103).

content.stem: In DOE, if one factor is proven to affect the performance of a second factor, it is known as which of the following?
content.why: Interaction effect is when one factor is proven to affect the performance of a second factor in DoE. A main effect is present in DOE when different levels of a factor are shown to affect the response differently. C. Interaction effect Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Improve Phase, Question 10 (PDF p. 103).

options: Amount of liquid absorbed by a paper towel
content.stem: Which of the following is an example of a dependent variable?
content.why: The amount of liquid that is absorbed by a paper towel is an example of a dependent variable. In this example, the amount of liquid absorbed is an outcome which would be affected by changes to an independent variable, such as the brand of paper towel used. A. Amount of liquid absorbed by a paper towel Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Improve Phase, Question 11 (PDF p. 103).

content.stem: Which of the following is a method used to assist with root cause analysis?
content.why: Brainstorming is a method used to assist with root cause analysis. SMED is a tool used to assist with cycle-time reduction. D. Brainstorming Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Improve Phase, Question 12 (PDF p. 103).

content.stem: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of continuous flow?
content.why: Lower inventory levels is a benefit of continuous flow. Together with decreased bottlenecks, increased throughput, and shorter cycle time these benefits help to eliminate waste in a process by improving movement and flow within the process. B. Higher inventory levels Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Improve Phase, Question 13 (PDF p. 103).

content.stem: The elapsed time from the last good unit of one product to the first good unit of the next product is known as which of the following?
content.why: Setup time is the elapsed time from the last good unit of the outgoing product to the first good unit of the next product on the process. Setup-reduction methods such as SMED aim to shorten this changeover interval. C. Setup time Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Improve Phase, Question 14 (PDF p. 104).

options: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, and Control (DMAIC)
content.sourceSection: Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: For a company working to improve an existing process, what’s the most well-known and frequently used project methodology?
content.why: DMAIC is the standard improvement roadmap for an existing process; DFSS methods are used for new or redesigned products and processes. C. Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, and Control (DMAIC) Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 8 (PDF p. 28).

options: A Kaizen blitz focuses on rapidly correcting one issue, while Kaizen focuses on ongoing small changes to improve processes.
A Kaizen blitz does not encourage employee contributions, and Kaizen does.
A Kaizen blitz is made up of three stages, while Kaizen is made up of twenty steps.
There is no major difference between Kaizen and a Kaizen blitz.
content.stem: Which of the following is the major difference between a Kaizen blitz and Kaizen?
content.why: A Kaizen blitz is a short, concentrated event aimed at rapid results; Kaizen is the broader ongoing philosophy of continuous improvement. A. A Kaizen blitz focuses on rapidly correcting one issue, while Kaizen focuses on ongoing small changes to improve processes. Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Improve Phase, Question 15 (PDF p. 104).

options: Use subgroups of 5 and X-bar and R charts to track weight variation.
Grouping the samples by 100 and using Excel’s Box Cox function to track variations in weight
Manually weighing each bag and using P control charts to track variations in weight
Linearly plotting the weights of each bag and logging the function to track variations in weight
content.stem: Sandbag Company fills sandbags for coastal homeowners. The operations supervisor tracks bag weight with X-bar and S charts using subgroups of 20. How could the process also be monitored?
content.why: X-bar & R charts, like X-S charts, track variation within groups, but require a small sample size to be accurate. The Operations Supervisor could use X-bar & R charting in the event that he was unable to quickly calculate standard deviation for his X-S charts. A. Use subgroups of 5 and X-bar and R charts to track weight variation. Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Control Phase, Question 1 (PDF p. 117).

content.stem: If a stable process output is normally distributed and its control limits are set at ±3 standard deviations, approximately what percentage of observations is expected to fall between the limits?
content.why: For a normal distribution, approximately 99.73% of observations lie within ±3 standard deviations of the mean. Control status still requires checking for special-cause patterns, not merely counting points inside the limits. D. 99.7% Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Control Phase, Question 2 (PDF p. 117), clarified for statistical accuracy.

content.stem: Normal instances of variation caused by routine and uncontrollable practices of the workflow are referred to as which of the following?
content.why: Common-cause variation is the routine, inherent variation produced by the current process system, such as ordinary differences between trained operators or normal equipment wear. D. Common causes Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Control Phase, Question 3 (PDF p. 117).

content.stem: Abnormal, abrupt, and unpredictable instances of variation that result from non-routine circumstances are referred to as which of the following?
content.why: Special causes include power outages, natural disasters, and unexpectedly broken equipment. Common causes include routine instances of the workflow that can cause variation. B. Special causes Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Control Phase, Question 4 (PDF p. 117).

content.stem: Mike will record one continuous process measurement each day for approximately three months, so rational subgroups are not available. Which control chart should he use?
content.why: An I-MR chart is appropriate for continuous measurements collected one observation at a time when rational subgroups are unavailable. An np chart tracks numbers of defective units with a constant sample size, while a u chart tracks defects per unit when the opportunity or sample size can vary. C. I-MR chart Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Control Phase, Question 5 (PDF p. 117), clarified for control-chart accuracy.

content.stem: Defects-per-unit data follow a Poisson distribution. Especially when the average count is small, which shape is commonly observed?
content.why: Poisson counts are bounded at zero and are commonly right-skewed when the mean count is small; as the mean increases, the distribution becomes more nearly symmetric. A. Right skewedness Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Control Phase, Question 6 (PDF p. 117), clarified for statistical accuracy.

content.stem: Ashley works in a public health clinic and is asked to track the percentage of patients seen who have Medicare insurance. Which of the following tracking tools is appropriate?
content.why: P charts are best for instances with only two possible outcomes. In this instance, Ashley would track whether a patient had Medicare insurance. B. P chart Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Control Phase, Question 7 (PDF p. 118).

content.stem: Which kind of documentation may include the action step “Stop, correct, resume”?
content.why: A response plan defines what to do when a monitored process signals a problem. “Stop, correct, resume” is one possible prescribed reaction; the other listed documents do not define that action sequence. A. Response plan Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Control Phase, Question 8 (PDF p. 118).

content.stem: Jessi is heading a new unit of her company. The unit will be responsible for creating a hand-held communication device. One process flow that Jessi will personally oversee is packaging the device so it can be shipped without incurring damage. Jessi begins compiling a resource that explains how packaging will take place, who will be involved, what kind of tests the package will undergo, and how testing will be monitored. Which of the following is Jessi creating?
content.why: A control plan documents the process flow, responsibilities, tests, monitoring method, and reaction controls needed to sustain performance. D. Control plan Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Control Phase, Question 9 (PDF p. 118).

options: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, and Control (DMAIC)
content.sourceSection: Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: Which approach do companies take when they need to create or redesign a product or process from the ground up to meet Six Sigma quality levels?
content.why: Design for Six Sigma (DFSS) is an approach that companies take when they need to create or redesign a product or process from the ground up that meets Six Sigma quality levels. Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, and Control (DMAIC) is the most well-known and frequently used project methodology for a company working to improve an existing process. D. Design for Six Sigma (DFSS) Source: Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide, Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 9 (PDF p. 28).

content.sourcePart: Part B: Practice Exam
content.stem: A production team consists of seven workers. How many ways can two workers be chosen to serve on an improvement team?
content.why: Two workers are selected without regard to order, so use C(7,2) = 7!/(2!5!) = 21. C. 21 Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part B Practice Exam, Question 100 (print p. 171), III.B.1.

options: Customers are demanding the use of Six Sigma in many industries.

Managers demand that Green Belts be trained to support organizations in today’s businesses.

content.sourceSection: I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: Why is Six Sigma important in a business application?
content.why: The true value of Six Sigma is the bottom-line results gained by an organization. B. Organizations must stay profitable to remain in business, and Six Sigma is a powerful tool to that end. Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 1 (print p. 4), I.A.1.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.sourceSection: I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: What is the main goal of the Six Sigma philosophy?
content.why: The threads common to the Six Sigma philosophy are found in Chapter 1 of The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Handbook, with the best choice of this group being to reduce variation. The other three are true and can be counted as subsets or results of reducing variation in a process, as Deming and Juran have suggested in their writings. A. Reduced variation Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 2 (print p. 4), I.A.1.

options: Failure to properly define the processes to be utilized in the organization

Too many organizational definitions of what Six Sigma should be
Management’s lack of commitment to real process improvement

content.sourceSection: I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: What is the most common cause of a failed Six Sigma program in an organization?
content.why: The lack of management commitment and involvement has led to a very large failure rate for Six Sigma implementation. The use of Deming’s Fourteen Points, the Management’s Seven Deadly Diseases, or Juran’s Trilogy could help in this regard. D. Management’s lack of commitment to real process improvement Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 3 (print p. 4), I.A.1.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.sourceSection: I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: The person who first developed the concept of what we call statistical process control (SPC) was:
content.why: Shewhart created the control chart in the 1920s, and Bell Labs coined the term statistical quality control. The first control chart developed by Shewhart was the P Chart. D. Walter A. Shewhart. Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 4 (print p. 5), I.A.1.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.sourceSection: I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: The cause-and-effect, or fishbone, diagram was created by:
content.why: Also called the Ishikawa diagram. Note: Deming tried to Americanize this tool by calling it a feather diagram, but the term never stuck. Taguchi is most known for the loss function and design of experiments (DOEs) using orthogonal arrays. C. Kaoru Ishikawa. Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 5 (print p. 5), I.A.1.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.sourceSection: I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: The quality guru who wrote extensively about the three key managerial processes (quality planning, quality control, and quality improvement) was:
content.why: Juran wrote a great deal on issues of management over his long career. Note that he was introduced to this by watching the Hawthorne experiments as they developed at the Western Electric plant in Cicero, IL, when he was a young quality engineer. B. Joseph M. Juran. Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 6 (print p. 5), I.A.1.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.sourceSection: I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: Which of the following tools is a process approach used for improving projects?
content.why: The inputs-process-output (IPO) model is the starting point of a flow diagram that will define a process. Plan-do-check-act (PDCA) is used more as a cycle analysis; however, the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) community recognizes this in the management system standards (MSS) as a form of a process. Both a and b are tools used in Six Sigma but are not process-approach tools. PDCA is a problem-solving tool. The IPO is a process-approach tool. D. Input-process-output (IPO) Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 7 (print p. 5), I.A.1.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.sourceSection: I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: Which element of SMART goals ensures that the goal is realistic and attainable?
content.why: The A in SMART goals stands for achievable. Given available resources and constraints, the goal should be realistic and feasible. C. Achievable Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 8 (print p. 5), I.A.2.

options: Ensuring only appropriate goals are met
Assessing an organization’s position before deciding on any new strategy

content.stem: SMART goals have become increasingly popular for what use?
content.why: Project management has been using SMART goals for many years. D. Assessing project management Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 9 (print p. 6), I.A.2.

content.sourcePart: Part B: Practice Exam
content.stem: Which graphic tool is best for developing a complete picture of the relationship between two variables?
content.why: A scatter plot is the graphic tool best used for developing a complete picture of the relationship between two variables. D. Scatter plot Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part B Practice Exam, Question 10 (print p. 150), IV.A.2.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.sourceSection: I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: SMART goals are also known as:
content.why: The use of SMART goals is to provide objectives for the team to meet when working through projects. A. objectives. Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 10 (print p. 6), I.A.2.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.sourceSection: I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: What does KPI stand for in standard ASQ quality terminology?
content.why: KPI is the standard abbreviation for Key Performance Indicator. The book keys Key Process Indicator, but that expansion conflicts with ASQ's standard quality terminology; the student-facing key is corrected here. A. Key Performance Indicator Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 11 (print p. 6), I.A.3.

options: It is a quantifiable measurement, agreed to in advance, that reflects critical success factors.

content.stem: Which of the following statements describes a KPI?
content.why: Remember that we are looking at processes, so ensuring quantifiable measurement is the key to answering this question. Both b and c are distractors that come from the SMART goal concepts. A. It is a quantifiable measurement, agreed to in advance, that reflects critical success factors. content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.sourceSection: I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization
content.stem: Sorting through all the data being collected and identifying the key measures to track are key challenges for any organization. Who is responsible for guiding the measures tracked in projects?
content.why: The management team or project champions should be setting the boundaries for the Six Sigma team, even when there are Master Black Belts involved. Setting boundaries also helps to prevent “scope creep.” B. The management team gives direction on what measures are tracked in projects. Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A I. Overview: Six Sigma and the Organization, Question 13 (print p. 6), I.A.3.

Selecting KPIs that are easy to measure but unrelated to goals

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.stem: When throwing a standard six-sided die, what is the probability of getting a 4 or a 6?

content.stem: What is the formula for the probability of Event A or B occurring when the events are mutually exclusive?
content.why: Using the general addition rule, P(A) + P(B) − P(A & B). If Events A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A and B) = 0. Therefore, the formula reduces to P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). A. P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A III. Measure Phase, Question 10 (print p. 48), III.B.1.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.stem: There are two extrusion machines that produce plastic parts. Forty percent of the parts are produced on Machine A. The probability that a randomly chosen part is made on Machine A and is defective is 0.02. What is the probability that a part is defective given that it is made on Machine A?
content.why: Use conditional probability: P(Defective | Machine A) = P(Machine A and Defective) / P(Machine A) = 0.02 / 0.40 = 0.05. B. 0.05 Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A III. Measure Phase, Question 11 (print p. 48), III.B.1.

B. 15/100 Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A III. Measure Phase, Question 12 (print p. 49), III.B.1.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.stem: What is the probability that a complaint involves a shipping concern?
content.why: There are two types of shipping complaints: shipping damage and lost shipment. The total number of these complaints is 23 + 10 = 33. Therefore, P(Shipping complaint) = 33/100. C. 33/100 Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A III. Measure Phase, Question 13 (print p. 49), III.B.1.

content.sourcePart: Part B: Practice Exam
content.stem: Which graphical tool provides a pictorial view of numerical data about location and spread?

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.stem: What is the probability that a connector complaint concerns missing connectors?
content.why: The probability that a connector complaint concerns missing connectors is found using the conditional probability formula. Let P(Connector complaint) = P(A) and P(Missing connector) = P(B). We then can calculate: P(Missing | Connector) = 32 / 47. C. 32/47 Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A III. Measure Phase, Question 14 (print p. 49), III.B.1.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.stem: There are 15 inspection reports stored in a file folder. How many ways can five reports be chosen for an audit?
content.why: Five reports will be chosen from 15, in no particular order. We can use the combination formula to solve using n = 15 and r = 5. C(15,5) = 15! / [5!(15−5)!] = 3003. C. 3003 Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A III. Measure Phase, Question 15 (print p. 49), III.B.1.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.stem: How many ways can a group of 20 candidates be assigned to the chair, vice-chair, and secretary positions of a volunteer organization?
content.why: Three candidates will be chosen for different positions, so order matters here. Using the permutation formula with n = 20 and r = 3 yields: P(20,3) = 20! / (20−3)! = 6840. D. 6840 Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A III. Measure Phase, Question 16 (print p. 50), III.B.1.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.stem: The distribution of averages tends to be normal, even when the distribution from which the averages are computed is not normal. This statement is a consequence of the:
content.why: The central limit states that averages tend to be normally distributed, even if the original distribution is not normally distributed. D. central limit theorem. Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A III. Measure Phase, Question 17 (print p. 50), III.B.2.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.stem: Samples of size 36 are taken from a skewed population with a mean equal to 10.0 and a standard deviation equal to 10.0. The sample averages will follow which distribution?
content.why: This is an application of the central limit theorem. The sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal with mean μ = 10 and standard error σ/√n = 10/√36 = 1.667. C. Normal with μ = 10, σ = 1.667 Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A III. Measure Phase, Question 18 (print p. 50), III.B.2.

Measure Phase, Question 19 (print p. 50), III.B.2.

content.stem: A Green Belt performs a chi-square goodness-of-fit test with alpha = 0.05 to determine whether the distribution of defect types last month differed from the historical percentages. Given the data table below, which statement is true?
content.why: The expected counts are 70, 35, and 35. χ² = (60−70)²/70 + (35−35)²/35 + (45−35)²/35 = 4.286. With df = 3−1 = 2 and α = 0.05, the critical value is 5.991. B. The test statistic = 4.286, and the critical value = 5.991. Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part B Practice Exam, Question 24 (print p. 153), IV.B.2.

Student’s t Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A III. Measure Phase, Question 28 (print p. 52), III.C.

content.stem: Which distribution is used to test the ratio of two variances?
content.why: We test the ratio of two variances using the F distribution. D. F Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A III. Measure Phase, Question 29 (print p. 52), III.C.

content.stem: Which distribution is used to test a standard deviation against a standard?
content.why: The chi-square distribution is used to test a variance or standard deviation against a standard. B. Chi-square Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A III. Measure Phase, Question 30 (print p. 53), III.C.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.stem: A sample of size six is randomly selected from a batch with a 10% defective rate. Find the probability that the sample has exactly one defective.
content.why: For X ~ Binomial(n = 6, p = 0.10), P(X = 1) = C(6,1)(0.10)(0.90)⁵ = 0.354294, which rounds to 0.3543. The book's printed key says 0.3281 even though its displayed calculation gives 0.3543; the student-facing key is corrected here. B. 0.3543 Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A III. Measure Phase, Question 31 (print p. 53), III.C.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.stem: An electronic component manufacturer has an average defect rate of 0.01 per unit. What is the probability that an inspector finds one or fewer defects in a sample of 100 units?
content.why: This is an application of the Poisson distribution in which we are counting defects per unit. If there are an average of 0.01 defects per unit, we should expect (0.01)(100) = 1 defect per 100 units. We can use the Poisson distribution with λ = 1. To find the probability of finding one or zero defects in 100 units: P(X ≤ 1) = e⁻¹ + e⁻¹ = 0.7358. C. 0.7358 Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A III. Measure Phase, Question 32 (print p. 53), III.C.

content.sourcePart: Part A: Sample Questions by BoK
content.stem: A normal distribution can be standardized using which transformation?
content.why: The Z transformation standardizes any normal distribution with a mean μ and variance σ² into a standard normal with mean equal to 0 and variance equal to 1. Note: Z = (X−μ) / σ. A. Z Source: The ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt Study Guide (2024), Part A III. Measure Phase, Question 33 (print p. 53), III.C.

content.sourcePart: Part B: Practice Exam
content.stem: Which of the following subgroup sizes for an X-bar and R chart would most likely be used if measurement were costly?
